summary:
Section 198 of Brunei's Syariah Penal Code creates the trans-specific offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa", qualified in the statute by acting "without reasonable excuse" or "for immoral purposes". Official guidance on the code states that it binds all persons in the country including tourists, and travel agents are briefed to that effect.

Human Rights Watch's #OUTLAWED survey places Brunei among at least two countries, with Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex; Malaysia has a state-sharia analogue.

Brunei does not permit a person to change their name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not allowed. A trans visitor should therefore expect to cross the border on a passport whose sex marker and name cannot be aligned with presentation, under a statute that criminalises mismatched presentation.

Enforcement of the cross-dressing provision is documented but thin. The US State Department's 2017 report on human rights practices records no known convictions under the provision that year, while noting that morality provisions including cross-dressing were among those actually enforced under the code and that the sharia implementing regulations had not yet been issued. On 11 March 2015 a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing.

Official conduct toward LGBT people is adverse in ways a visitor may encounter directly. LGBTI individuals reported intimidation by police, including threats to disclose their sexuality, interference with access to government employment, and barriers to graduation from government academic institutions. Members of the community also reported that the government monitored their activities and communications.

Events on LGBT topics were subject to restrictions on assembly and expression, with the government reportedly refusing to issue permits for them. LGBTI respondents separately reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and access to services.

The statutory severity is high. If evidentiary standards under the Syariah Penal Code Order are not met, the maximum penalty for sex between men is seven years' imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping; for unmarried men, one year in prison or 100 lashes; and sex between women is punishable by any two of forty lashes of caning, up to ten years' imprisonment, and a fine of up to B$40,000. Anyone convicted of "tarnishing the image of Islam" may also be heavily punished.
tangentialFactors:
Stage 3 of the Syariah Penal Code took effect on 3 April 2019, introducing death by stoning for anal sex and adultery, amputation for theft, and 40 strokes of the cane for lesbian sex. The stoning penalties extend to anal sex and adultery and, by the account of the UK House of Commons Library, to abortion; homosexuality was already an offence carrying up to ten years under the prior law.

The code applies in the main to Muslims, who make up roughly two-thirds of a population reported at between 420,000 and 450,000. The head of state stated that the capital-punishment moratorium covers the new sharia penal code, and the moratorium on executions has held; Brunei has carried out no execution since 1957. Freshness checks in September 2026 indicate the 2019 moratorium remains intact.

The code drew condemnation from the UN High Commissioner, who urged Brunei to halt it, from Human Rights Watch, which called it barbaric, and from international media, which described the sharia provisions as medieval and uncivilized. OutRight Action International has described Brunei as the country with the most worrisome state of rights for LGBT people in its region.

Bruneian society tends to associate homosexuality with effeminate men, a cultural association that raises the profile of gender-nonconforming presentation independently of the statute. First-person reporting at the time of stage 3 describes a climate of fear among LGBT residents, with sources speaking anonymously and no assurance that enforcement would be confined to residents rather than foreigners.
localsOnly:
The 11 March 2015 cross-dressing prosecution involved a civil servant, indicating that the provision has been applied inside state employment rather than only against passers-by. Residents also face employment and housing discrimination, restrictions on government jobs, and barriers to graduation from government academic institutions.

Government monitoring of the activities and communications of LGBT residents is reported, alongside police threats to make a person's sexuality public. Permits for events on LGBT topics are reportedly refused, constraining assembly and expression for resident organisers.

Document rules bind residents permanently: neither name nor gender marker may be changed on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not available domestically. Community members also describe social conflation of homosexuality with effeminate presentation, which shapes day-to-day exposure beyond formal enforcement.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources in the inventory could not be retrieved at research time: the hosted text of Brunei's Penal Code, including the Syariah Penal Code provisions, returned HTTP 403, as did an SSRN paper on the sharia penal code. The precise current wording of Section 198 is therefore taken from secondary description rather than the statute itself, and the qualified phrases "without reasonable excuse" and "for immoral purposes" are not independently verified against the primary text.

Whether the sharia implementing regulations referenced as unissued in the 2017 US State Department report have since been promulgated is unresolved in the available sources; the same report's cross-dressing enforcement picture predates the 2019 stage-3 commencement by two years.

Unresolved: whether Section 198 has been charged against foreign nationals since 2015, and whether Brunei's immigration authorities screen or annotate passports on gender grounds. Neither point is sourced in the inventory. The claim that official guidance binds tourists rests on guidance material cited in the record, not on a published enforcement case.

Whether the execution moratorium would hold if a stoning sentence were pronounced against a non-Muslim is not addressed by the sources; they state only that the moratorium covers the new code and that no execution has been carried out since 1957.
